children: It may be Stephen is thinking of the literati in the library, it may be of those he encounters everywhere in his journeying, but he hurls the word, “Stop” at beingless beings, soulless shells of humanity. “You sing of your heart, well let me tell you about my heart,” he seems to say. There are a number of dichotomies over which Stephen agonizes.  There are enduring heart throbbings from without and those from within. the heart being the repository of the most intense, stirring personal longings and emotions perhaps those from without for Stephen are for artistic and professional success as a writer/poet, acceptance by those who had just dismissed him earlier that day, and those yearnings from within, those involving the most enduring longings, those for unity with the three entities from which he had emotionally exiled himself, viz. God, family, and country, a return to unity with which was his private, probably subconscious odyssey. Immanuel Kant taught that there are two ways of
seeing

the world; we can see it either as a world as it appears, or as a world as it is in itself, but which we cannot see due to our human limitations. Martin Buber saw that, implicit in Kant’s views, there were two ways of
being
in the world. The first way is choose life in its fullness here and now, to
encounter
it in its wholeness. The other is to live in the world of things including the persons one experience as mere things.
